translation: Charge the adaptor Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases use ATP to attach the appropriate amino acid to a tRNA. The tRNA anticodon pairs with a codon, but that pairing does not itself verify the attached amino acid. Correct charging is a separate fidelity step. Read the message The ribosome reads mRNA in nonoverlapping triplets from 5′ to 3′. Many amino acids have multiple codons, making the code degenerate. A reading frame establishes which triplets are interpreted; shifting it changes downstream meaning. Elongate and terminate Charged tRNA enters, peptide bonds form, and the ribosome advances along the message. The chain grows from amino terminus to carboxyl terminus. Stop codons recruit release factors rather than an ordinary aminoacyl-tRNA.
genetic-testing: Define what needs detection A single-nucleotide change, repeat expansion, copy-number alteration and methylation change are different targets. No single routine method detects all classes equally well. The question and suspected mechanism should come before the choice of instrument. Compare method scope PCR amplifies a defined region. Sanger sequencing reads a relatively limited sequence; massively parallel methods examine many regions but still have coverage constraints. Chromosomal microarrays detect copy-number imbalance and generally do not detect balanced rearrangements or most individual base substitutions. Interpret the evidence A result must be considered with phenotype, inheritance, specimen and assay limitations. A variant of uncertain significance is not a confirmed causal diagnosis. A negative result only addresses abnormalities the method could detect in the tested sample.
complement: Converge on C3 Classical, lectin and alternative pathways begin differently but produce C3-cleaving activity. Classical initiation often involves antibody-containing complexes; lectin recognition detects carbohydrate patterns; the alternative pathway contributes activation and amplification on suitable surfaces. Separate the outputs C3b and related fragments promote opsonization. C3a and C5a participate in inflammatory signaling, with C5a an important chemoattractant. C5b initiates formation of the C5b–9 membrane-attack complex. These fragments have distinct functions despite similar names. Protect host tissue Complement needs regulation to avoid indiscriminate injury. CD55 accelerates convertase decay, while CD59 limits terminal complex assembly. Other soluble and membrane regulators act at earlier steps. Uncontrolled amplification can damage host cells as well as targets. Explain why activating complement and limiting complement are both necessary. Activation labels and attacks targets and recruits responses. Regulation limits amplification and terminal injury on host surfaces, preserving useful defense without uncontrolled tissue damage. Why can different complement activation pathways have common downstream effects? They converge on C3 activation and shared downstream components. Convergence explains shared effects such as C3b-mediated opsonisation despite different triggers.
hypersensitivity-mechanisms: Start with the cause of injury Hypersensitivity describes immune responses that cause tissue damage. The traditional four-type framework organises mechanisms; a real disorder can involve more than one. Classification requires identifying antigen location, effector molecules or cells, and the process causing injury. The words rapid and delayed are clues, but timing by itself is not a complete mechanism. Do not call every inflammatory response IgE-mediated allergy. Connect IgE with a sensitised mast cell In type I reactions, antigen cross-links specific IgE already bound to high-affinity receptors on mast cells or basophils. This triggers mediator release and subsequent inflammatory events. Sensitisation and the later effector response are distinct stages. An immediate component can be followed by later inflammation, so a later phase does not automatically convert the response into type IV. The key is the IgE-linked activation pathway. Distinguish the two antibody patterns Type II involves antibodies directed against cell-surface or extracellular-matrix targets. Effects can include complement activation, phagocyte-mediated injury or altered receptor function; cell destruction is not the only possible result. Type III involves antigen–antibody complexes whose deposition and associated inflammation injure tissues. Ask whether the antibody targets a fixed structure directly or whether complexes form and deposit. Both may recruit complement, so complement alone cannot separate them. Recognise a T-cell effector response Type IV responses are mediated principally by antigen-specific T cells. CD4 T-cell cytokines can recruit and activate inflammatory cells, while CD8 T cells can injure target cells directly. Contact dermatitis is a classic teaching context. The time needed for recruitment helps explain a delayed response, but the defining feature is the effector mechanism. Naming a cytokine or a time interval without identifying the cells leaves the explanation incomplete. Identify the effector rather than classify by timing alone. Separate fixed-target antibodies from deposited immune complexes. Explain why type IV does not require antibody as its principal effector. Classify an original comparison case Case A: antibody binds a receptor and changes its function. Case B: soluble antigen–antibody complexes deposit and recruit inflammatory cells. Case C: sensitised T cells drive local inflammation after contact exposure. A follows a type II mechanism because antibody acts against a fixed target; receptor effects need not lyse the cell. B follows a type III mechanism because deposited complexes drive the injury. C follows a type IV mechanism because T cells are the principal specific effectors.
inheritance: State the model Under a simple autosomal dominant model, a heterozygous parent and a partner without the variant give each child a one-half chance of inheriting it. Under a simple autosomal recessive model, two heterozygous parents give a one-quarter chance of an affected genotype per pregnancy. Separate inheritance from expression Penetrance describes whether a genotype manifests the associated phenotype. Expressivity describes variation in features or severity among those who express it. Inheriting a variant and showing a specific clinical picture are therefore different events. Explain exceptions before discarding the model De novo variants, reduced penetrance, mosaicism and limited family size can obscure an expected pedigree pattern. Probability applies separately to each conception under the specified assumptions; previous outcomes do not force the next child’s result.
innate-adaptive: Begin at the barrier Epithelial junctions, mucus, antimicrobial products and controlled flow reduce access to tissues. Innate sensors recognize conserved microbial patterns or signs of cell damage. Their location helps define which compartment is being monitored. Recruit an immediate response Phagocytes ingest material and inflammatory signals recruit additional cells. Natural killer cells integrate activating and inhibitory signals to assess potential targets. Dendritic cells connect local antigen capture to activation of naive T cells. Build a specific response B- and T-cell populations carry diverse antigen receptors generated during development. Antigen-driven selection expands relevant clones and can establish memory. Adaptive responses rely on innate instructions, while antibodies and T cells can in turn strengthen innate effector functions.
meiosis: Replicate once, divide twice Meiosis follows one round of DNA replication with two divisions. Homologous chromosomes separate in meiosis I; sister chromatids separate in meiosis II. Crossing-over and independent assortment contribute to genetically varied gametes. Locate the segregation error Nondisjunction is failure of the expected chromosome separation. The consequences depend on which division fails. Distinguish adding or losing an individual chromosome from adding an entire chromosome set; aneuploidy and polyploidy are different categories. Ask when the error occurred A postzygotic mitotic error can create genetically different cell populations within one individual. This is mosaicism. Which tissues contain a cell line and how many cells are affected influence both detection and biological consequences.
antigen-presentation: Class I: inspect intracellular material The conventional class I pathway presents peptides generated from cytosolic proteins. Proteasomal processing and TAP transport support loading in the ER. CD8 T cells recognize peptide–MHC I complexes displayed on another cell. Class II: inspect vesicular material Professional antigen-presenting cells process material in vesicular compartments and display peptides on class II. CD4 T cells recognize peptide–MHC II complexes. The antigen-presenting cell displays the peptide; the T cell is the recognizing partner. Add activation context Recognition alone is not the complete naive-T-cell activation program. Co-stimulation and cytokines help determine the response. Cross-presentation also allows some extracellular material to enter class I presentation, so peptide source rules need appropriate qualification.
recessive-conditional-probability: Define the model before calculating Let A be a functional allele and a a disease-associated recessive allele. In a simplified single-gene model, both parents are known heterozygotes Aa. Each contributes A or a with probability one half, independently of the other parent. The four equally likely transmissions produce AA, Aa, aA and aa. Aa and aA describe the same heterozygous genotype, but arise from two different transmission combinations. Distinguish the initial probabilities Before any phenotype information about a child, the genotype probabilities are one quarter AA, one half heterozygous and one quarter aa. Under the stated complete-penetrance model, aa is affected and the other three transmission outcomes are unaffected. These are probabilities for each pregnancy. An affected earlier child does not mechanically use up the affected outcome for a later pregnancy; independent transmissions do not follow a quota. Condition on what is now known If the child is known to be unaffected under this model, the aa outcome is excluded. Three equally likely original transmission outcomes remain: AA, Aa and aA. Two represent carriers. Therefore carrier probability among unaffected children is two thirds, not one half. The denominator changed from all outcomes to the outcomes compatible with the observation. This is an application of conditional probability, not a new rule of meiosis. Respect the model limits The calculation assumes the parental genotypes, the disease model and reliable phenotype classification. Age-dependent or incomplete penetrance can prevent an unaffected observation from excluding aa. Variant interpretation, testing limitations and different genetic mechanisms also matter. A negative test updates probability according to its detection properties; it is not automatically the same evidence as an unaffected phenotype. These exercises teach reasoning and are not individual genetic-risk assessments. Construct the Aa × Aa outcome space. Calculate carrier probability after excluding affected outcomes. State the assumptions before applying a Mendelian calculation. Add a known carrier partner An unaffected child of two known Aa parents later has a partner known to be Aa. Within the same simplified model, calculate the probability that their child is aa. The unaffected individual has carrier probability 2/3. If that individual is Aa, an Aa × Aa cross has aa probability 1/4. Multiply: (2/3) × (1/4) = 1/6. The calculation assumes the same locus, complete penetrance and the stated parental and partner genotypes.
vessel-histology: Use the three tunics The intima includes endothelium; the media contains smooth muscle and elastic components; the adventitia provides outer connective-tissue support. Large vessels may contain small nourishing vessels in their walls. Not every vessel displays all layers equally clearly. Compare arteries with veins Elastic arteries have numerous elastic lamellae in the media. Muscular arteries have a prominent smooth-muscle media. A companion vein usually has a larger, less regular lumen and a thinner media, but collapse and cutting angle can alter these appearances. Find the exchange surface Capillaries are principally endothelial tubes supported by basal lamina, with associated pericytes in many locations. They lack a continuous muscular media. Arterioles, by contrast, have a smooth-muscle cuff that can regulate resistance and downstream flow.
blood-marrow: Orient the specimen A blood smear spreads circulating cells into a thin layer. Marrow is a tissue containing mixed developing cells, vascular sinusoids, adipocytes and supporting stroma. A smear and a marrow section answer different identification questions. Use a combination of clues Mature erythrocytes are anucleate; neutrophils have segmented nuclei; eosinophils have prominent eosinophilic granules. Small lymphocytes often have a dense round nucleus with scant cytoplasm, but morphology alone does not reliably distinguish B cells from T cells. Trace production Marrow stem and progenitor populations give rise to blood-cell lineages. Very large megakaryocytes produce platelets by cytoplasmic fragmentation. Erythroid maturation progressively condenses the nucleus and increases hemoglobin before the nucleus is expelled.
cartilage-bone: Recognize cartilage Chondrocytes occupy lacunae in a hydrated extracellular matrix. Hyaline cartilage contains fine type II collagen fibrils; elastic cartilage adds elastic fibers; fibrocartilage has conspicuous tensile collagen bundles. Cartilage is avascular and relies on diffusion for nutrition. Recognize bone Bone combines collagenous organic matrix with mineral. Osteoblasts form osteoid; osteocytes occupy lacunae and communicate through canaliculi; osteoclasts resorb bone. Compact bone often has osteons around vascular canals, while spongy bone forms trabeculae. Separate growth from replacement Intramembranous ossification forms bone directly in mesenchyme. Endochondral ossification replaces a cartilage model. Remodeling coordinates resorption and formation throughout life; osteoblast-lineage RANKL promotes osteoclast development, while osteoprotegerin limits that signal.
cell-junctions: Seal the route between cells Tight junctions regulate paracellular passage and help preserve apical-basal polarity. They are selective barriers rather than universal waterproof seals. A transporting epithelium can move substances through cells and, where permitted, between them. Anchor or communicate Adherens junctions connect actin networks between cells. Desmosomes connect intermediate filaments between cells; hemidesmosomes anchor cells to the basal lamina. Gap junction channels pass small molecules and ions between neighboring cells. Recognize the apical apparatus Microvilli contain actin and increase surface area for absorption. Motile cilia use microtubules and dynein to move material along a surface. Stereocilia are long actin-based microvilli, despite their name; they are not ordinary motile cilia.
connective-tissue: Look between the cells Connective tissue contains cells dispersed through extracellular matrix. Fibroblasts synthesize much of that matrix; immune cells may be resident or recruited. Compared with epithelium, the matrix is usually the more prominent organizing feature. Match material to a mechanical job Collagen resists tension, elastic fibers allow recoil, and proteoglycan-rich hydrated ground substance supports diffusion and resistance to compression. The amount and arrangement of these components matter as much as their names. Read the fiber arrangement Loose connective tissue provides flexible support beneath many epithelia. Dense regular tissue aligns collagen for tension mainly in one direction, as in tendon. Dense irregular tissue distributes collagen in multiple directions, helping structures such as dermis resist varied stresses.
epithelia: Find the two surfaces The apical surface faces a lumen or the outside. The basal surface rests on a basement membrane supported by connective tissue. Closely packed cells and relatively little extracellular matrix distinguish an epithelial sheet from its supporting stroma. Count layers, then name the surface cells Simple epithelium has one cell layer. Stratified epithelium has several and is named by the superficial cells. Pseudostratified epithelium appears multilayered because nuclei sit at different heights, but every cell contacts the basement membrane. Connect architecture to function Thin squamous cells suit exchange, as in alveoli. Cuboidal or columnar cells often support absorption and secretion. Multiple layers protect surfaces exposed to friction. Urothelium is a specialized stratified lining that accommodates urinary-tract distension. Simple cuboidal epithelium Pink kidney tissue with open tubular profiles encircled by cuboidal cells and rounded purple nuclei. Kidney tubule section, identified by the source as simple cuboidal epithelium at 200×. Follow the lining around a lumen. Screen size is not a calibrated scale; this view alone does not establish a specific nephron segment. Stratified squamous epithelium A thick epithelial lining curves around a pale lumen, with multiple cell layers and flattened cells at the free surface. Source-identified stratified squamous epithelium at 100×. Compare the multiple layers and superficial cell shape with the cuboidal section. The two images have different source magnifications; displayed sizes are not directly comparable. Why does alveolar epithelium differ from esophageal epithelium? Alveoli need a short diffusion distance and use thin squamous cells. The esophagus resists abrasion with a nonkeratinized stratified squamous lining. A section has nuclei at different heights, but every cell contacts the basal lamina. Which interpretation fits? Pseudostratified epithelium is possible. In pseudostratified epithelium all cells contact the basal lamina, although not all reach the surface.
respiratory-histology: Conduct and clear The trachea and larger conducting airways use ciliated epithelium and mucus-producing cells to move trapped material toward the pharynx. Cartilage and glands are useful clues to larger airways. The epithelial pattern changes as the airway narrows. Recognize a bronchiole Bronchioles lack cartilage and submucosal glands. Their relatively simple epithelium includes club cells, and smooth muscle helps regulate caliber. Terminal bronchioles remain conducting airways; respiratory bronchioles have alveoli interrupting their walls. Build an exchange barrier Type I pneumocytes form a thin gas-exchange surface. Type II pneumocytes produce surfactant and contribute to epithelial repair. The thin barrier combines alveolar epithelium, closely apposed basal laminae and capillary endothelium; macrophages clear particles within the alveolar region.
renal-histology: Find the cortex Renal corpuscles locate the cortex. Medulla contains straight tubules, loops and collecting ducts but lacks corpuscles. Medullary rays are straight tubular groups extending into cortex; their name does not place them in medulla. Separate filtration from transport The renal corpuscle combines a capillary tuft and Bowman capsule. Filtration crosses capillary endothelium, glomerular basement membrane and the podocyte slit apparatus. Filtrate then enters the tubular system rather than becoming final urine immediately. Compare tubular clues Proximal tubules have an apical brush border and often an indistinct lumen. Distal tubules have a clearer lumen and lack a prominent brush border. Collecting ducts tend to have more distinct cell boundaries. Identify a pattern across several profiles rather than trusting lumen size alone. Simple cuboidal epithelium Pink kidney tissue with open tubular profiles encircled by cuboidal cells and rounded purple nuclei. Kidney tubule section, identified by the source as simple cuboidal epithelium at 200×. Follow the lining around a lumen. Screen size is not a calibrated scale; this view alone does not establish a specific nephron segment.
liver-pancreas: Read the liver lobule Portal tracts contain branches of portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct. Blood from the two vascular inputs enters sinusoids and moves toward a central vein. Hepatocytes are arranged along those exchange channels. Reverse direction for bile Bile enters canaliculi between hepatocytes and flows toward ductules and ducts in portal regions. It does not normally drain into the central vein. Gallbladder stores and concentrates bile; it does not synthesize bile or digestive enzymes. Separate the pancreatic compartments Exocrine acini make digestive secretions that enter a duct system; centroacinar cells mark the beginning of that system. Endocrine islets release hormones into blood. Islets often appear paler than surrounding acini, but architecture and cell organization remain essential.
brain-and-csf-barriers: Trace blood toward brain interstitial fluid At typical CNS capillaries, endothelial cells are joined by tight junctions and show restricted nonspecific transcytosis. These endothelial properties form the principal blood–brain barrier. Crossing from blood to brain therefore requires an appropriate transcellular route for many substances. A barrier is selective rather than absolutely impermeable: oxygen can diffuse, and transport proteins support the regulated passage of needed nutrients. Place support cells around the endothelial seal Pericytes, basement membranes and astrocytic endfeet contribute to the neurovascular environment and maintenance of barrier properties. Astrocytes are important, but their endfeet are not the endothelial tight junctions themselves. When explaining a labelled drawing, distinguish the luminal endothelial lining from the cells and processes outside it. Saying that astrocytes simply form the seal hides the most important anatomical boundary. Take the choroid-plexus route separately Choroid-plexus capillaries are fenestrated. The blood–CSF barrier lies principally at tight junctions between the specialised choroid-plexus epithelial cells. These epithelial cells regulate the passage from the vascular connective-tissue core toward ventricular CSF. Thus the blood–brain route has an endothelial seal, whereas the choroid-plexus route has an epithelial seal. Ordinary ventricular ependyma should not be assigned the same tight barrier properties as the specialised choroid-plexus epithelium. Keep the glia limitans distinct Astrocytic endfeet and associated basal laminae contribute to the superficial glia limitans beneath the pia and to perivascular boundaries. These structures belong on a CNS barrier map but are not interchangeable with capillary endothelium. A routine light micrograph may show choroid-plexus fronds and epithelial lining but cannot directly resolve individual tight-junction strands. Connect visible architecture to mechanism while making the level of observation clear. Locate the sealing junctions in each barrier. Explain the contribution of astrocytes and pericytes. Distinguish ordinary ependyma from choroid-plexus epithelium. Follow a tracer into a choroid-plexus frond A schematic shows tracer passing out of a fenestrated capillary into the connective-tissue core, but not freely between epithelial cells into ventricular CSF. Identify the remaining boundary. The tracer has crossed the capillary wall in the choroid plexus. It still faces tight junctions between the specialised epithelial cells. This illustrates the blood–CSF barrier; it does not mean the blood–brain barrier is generally leaky.
lymphoid-organs: Lymph node: sample tissue lymph Afferent lymph reaches a subcapsular sinus before passing through the node. B-cell follicles occupy cortex, T cells are concentrated in paracortex, and medullary cords and sinuses form a different inner pattern. The organ brings transported antigen and lymphocytes together. Spleen: sample blood White pulp organizes lymphoid tissue around arteries. Red pulp contains cords and sinusoids involved in blood filtration and removal of poorly deformable erythrocytes. Unlike a lymph node, the spleen primarily monitors blood-borne material. Thymus: educate T cells Lobules have a dark cortex and lighter medulla. Medullary Hassall corpuscles are characteristic epithelial structures. Normal thymus does not have true lymphoid follicles; its principal role is T-cell development and selection rather than filtering afferent lymph.
myelin-and-glial-cells: Begin with location and relationships A supporting cell should be interpreted in its tissue context. Astrocytes regulate the neuronal environment, including extracellular potassium and transmitter handling. Oligodendrocytes form CNS myelin, while microglia are resident immune cells. Ependymal cells line most ventricular surfaces. In peripheral ganglia, satellite cells surround neuronal cell bodies. Schwann cells associate with peripheral axons. The word glia groups several distinct cell types rather than describing one universal support function. Count internodes rather than whole axons One myelinating Schwann cell forms one internode of one peripheral axon. A long axon therefore needs many successive Schwann cells. A single oligodendrocyte can extend processes to form internodes on several CNS axons. Nodes of Ranvier interrupt the myelin sheath and contain membrane specialised for regenerating the action potential. Myelin increases membrane resistance and reduces effective capacitance, helping local current spread toward the next node. Do not equate unmyelinated with unsupported Small peripheral axons can lie in grooves within a non-myelinating Schwann cell as a Remak bundle. They have Schwann-cell support without a compact multilamellar myelin sheath. Electrical conduction along axonal membrane is also different from axonal transport. Microtubule-based transport moves vesicles, proteins and organelles inside the axon; the propagation of a voltage change does not carry those materials down the nerve. Use the coverings to recognise a peripheral nerve In a transverse section, identify bundles bounded by perineurium before interpreting individual profiles. Endoneurial connective tissue lies among nerve fibres within a fascicle; epineurium surrounds and connects fascicles and contains larger vessels. Routine processing can dissolve myelin lipid, leaving pale rings or spaces. A single dark glial nucleus usually cannot establish a precise glial subtype without context or special methods. State what the preparation demonstrates and what remains inferred. Compare Schwann cells with oligodendrocytes. Distinguish myelination from axonal transport. Use tissue organisation to recognise a peripheral nerve. Reconstruct a nerve from a description A section shows several rounded fascicles, each with a concentric cellular boundary. Fine connective tissue surrounds individual fibres; thicker connective tissue lies between bundles. The boundary of each fascicle is perineurium. The delicate tissue within the fascicle is endoneurium. The tissue joining and surrounding fascicles is epineurium. These relations support peripheral-nerve identification. They do not by themselves prove the physiological class of each fibre.
neurulation: Induce and fold Signals from axial tissues including the notochord help organize overlying neural ectoderm. The neural plate forms a groove and elevated folds that meet to make the neural tube. This is a changing three-dimensional geometry, not a simple solid rod. Separate tube and crest The neural tube gives rise to the central nervous system. Neural crest cells leave the border region and migrate to diverse destinations, including many peripheral nervous-system structures. Do not use neural tube and neural crest as interchangeable names. Follow the wall layers The ventricular zone contains proliferating neuroepithelial cells. The mantle zone accumulates cell bodies and contributes gray matter; the marginal zone contains axons and contributes white matter. In the developing spinal cord, dorsal alar and ventral basal plates relate to sensory and motor organization.
placenta: Build a villus Primary villi are trophoblastic projections. Mesoderm entering the core produces secondary villi. Development of fetal vessels produces tertiary villi. This sequence connects a structural change to the establishment of fetal circulation within the exchange tissue. Keep the two circulations separate Maternal blood occupies the intervillous space and bathes villous surfaces. Fetal blood stays inside capillaries in the villous core. Exchange crosses intervening tissues; normal exchange does not require free mixing of the two blood pools. Understand what a barrier means The exchange barrier includes trophoblast, basal laminae, stroma and fetal endothelium, and becomes thinner as pregnancy advances. It is selective rather than absolute: some substances and pathogens cross. A structural barrier must not be interpreted as universal protection from exposure.
microscopy: Start at low power A section is a thin slice through a three-dimensional object. First find the outer boundary, lumen, capsule and repeating units. A tube cut obliquely may look oval or unusually thick; one isolated profile is rarely enough to identify an organ. Read the stain In routine hematoxylin and eosin, nuclei and other nucleic-acid-rich regions tend to be blue-purple, while many cytoplasmic proteins and collagen are pink. Staining intensity depends on preparation and does not directly measure cellular activity. Build a defensible identification Move to higher power to inspect nuclei, cell borders and matrix. State two positive features and one feature that separates the tissue from a look-alike. Folds, tears, shrinkage spaces and empty processing artifacts are not automatically normal structures. Simple cuboidal epithelium Pink kidney tissue with open tubular profiles encircled by cuboidal cells and rounded purple nuclei. Kidney tubule section, identified by the source as simple cuboidal epithelium at 200×. Follow the lining around a lumen. Screen size is not a calibrated scale; this view alone does not establish a specific nephron segment.
gi-histology: Name the common layers From the lumen outward, identify mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa and serosa or adventitia. The mucosa itself includes epithelium, lamina propria and muscularis mucosae. Do not confuse muscularis mucosae with the much larger muscularis externa. Identify the epithelial task Esophagus uses stratified squamous epithelium for abrasion resistance. Stomach has simple columnar surface cells, pits and glands. Small intestine adds villi and crypts; large intestine has numerous straight crypts and goblet cells but no normal villi. Use a regional discriminator Submucosal Brunner glands favor duodenum. Prominent villi and folds without Brunner glands or large aggregated lymphoid patches can favor jejunum. Aggregated lymphoid Peyer patches support ileum. Combine clues because a small or oblique section can miss defining structures.
reproductive-histology: Read a seminiferous tubule Developing germ cells progress from the basal region toward the lumen. Sertoli cells support this environment and form the blood-testis barrier. Leydig cells lie between tubules and produce testosterone. Sperm maturation continues after release into the duct system. Read an ovarian follicle An oocyte is surrounded by granulosa cells; developing follicles acquire additional layers and eventually an antrum. Ovulation is followed by luteinization of the residual follicular tissue. A corpus luteum is therefore a postovulatory endocrine structure, not an unfertilized egg. Read the endometrium in context Estrogen promotes proliferative growth. Progesterone supports a secretory endometrium with more tortuous glands. Cycle phase changes appearance, so an identification should distinguish organ identity from the hormonal state represented by the specimen.
muscle-histology: Skeletal muscle Long fibers have multiple peripheral nuclei and ordered sarcomeres that produce striations. Endomysium surrounds individual fibers, perimysium organizes fascicles, and epimysium surrounds the muscle. Section orientation can hide the longitudinal striation pattern. Cardiac muscle Branching striated cells usually have a central nucleus. Intercalated discs provide mechanical attachment through adherens junctions and desmosomes, and electrical coupling through gap junctions. These different junctions solve different problems at the same cell boundary. Smooth muscle Spindle-shaped cells have a central elongated nucleus and no sarcomeric cross-striations. Actin and myosin still generate force, but calcium-calmodulin activation of myosin light-chain kinase differs from the troponin-based control of striated muscle.
renal-tubular-transport: Recover the bulk early The proximal tubule normally reabsorbs roughly two-thirds of filtered sodium and water, most filtered bicarbonate, and nearly all glucose and amino acids at ordinary plasma concentrations. Water follows solute, so this bulk recovery is approximately isosmotic. Basolateral Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase supports many apical transport processes. Dilute, then fine-tune The thick ascending limb reabsorbs Na⁺, K⁺ and Cl⁻ through NKCC2 while remaining poorly permeable to water. The early distal convoluted tubule uses NCC. Later segments use channels including ENaC; principal cells couple sodium recovery to regulated potassium secretion. Transporters have limits Carrier-mediated glucose reabsorption can become saturated, allowing glucose to remain in urine. Glucose clearance rises when excretion begins, but that is a statement about glucose handling. It does not directly specify the urine’s total osmolality, which depends on all urinary solutes and water. Explain bulk proximal reabsorption. Locate NKCC2, NCC and ENaC. Distinguish transport saturation from changes in water handling.
renal-afferent-efferent: The inlet resistor Increasing afferent resistance reduces blood entry and lowers glomerular capillary pressure. Renal blood flow and GFR usually fall together. Afferent dilation has the opposite tendency when the other determinants are held constant. The outlet resistor Moderate efferent constriction reduces renal plasma flow but raises upstream glomerular hydrostatic pressure. GFR may rise or be maintained, increasing filtration fraction. With severe constriction, the large fall in plasma flow and the rise in glomerular capillary oncotic pressure can reduce GFR. More constriction does not mean indefinitely more filtration. Autoregulation is a response, not a second circuit Afferent smooth muscle contracts when stretched: the myogenic response buffers changes in perfusion pressure. Increased NaCl delivery to the macula densa promotes tubuloglomerular feedback that increases afferent tone. Low delivery favors renin release and reduced constrictor signaling. These responses modify a connected circulation. Predict the effects of afferent constriction. Explain moderate versus severe efferent constriction. Connect myogenic and macula-densa signals to afferent tone.
alveolar-ventilation-calculations: Separate total movement from useful ventilation Minute ventilation is tidal volume multiplied by breathing frequency. It measures the air moved at the airway opening per minute. Some air fills conducting passages and does not exchange gas with blood. In a simple model, alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume − dead-space volume) × frequency. Use the same units for both volumes. The expression describes effective ventilation only as well as the dead-space estimate represents the non-exchanging volume. Distinguish the two sources of dead space Anatomical dead space is the conducting-airway volume. Alveolar dead space represents ventilation reaching alveoli with absent or inadequate perfusion. Physiological dead space combines the two. The fixed anatomical value used in a classroom exercise is an assumption, not a universal patient measurement. A ventilation–perfusion disturbance may change physiological dead space even when conducting-airway anatomy has not changed. Compare patterns at the same minute ventilation For each breath, dead-space filling is paid before the remainder contributes to alveolar ventilation. When tidal volume is small, that cost takes a larger fraction of each breath. Increasing frequency can preserve minute ventilation while alveolar ventilation falls. This explains why the total litres breathed per minute cannot by itself tell you how effectively carbon dioxide is being removed. State the assumptions of the carbon dioxide prediction At steady state, arterial carbon dioxide tension varies approximately with carbon dioxide production divided by alveolar ventilation. If production is unchanged and alveolar ventilation halves, carbon dioxide tension tends to double. The relationship is a physiological model, not an instruction for setting a ventilator. Changing metabolism, non-steady-state conditions and altered gas exchange can make a simple numerical prediction inappropriate. Oxygenation also depends on inspired oxygen and gas-exchange matching, not ventilation alone. Calculate minute and alveolar ventilation. Explain why rapid shallow breaths waste more ventilation. Use the inverse relationship between alveolar ventilation and carbon dioxide cautiously. Same total ventilation, different result Compare pattern A: 500 mL × 12/min and pattern B: 250 mL × 24/min. Assume a fixed 150 mL dead space. Both patterns give minute ventilation of 6,000 mL/min, or 6 L/min. A: (500 − 150) × 12 = 4,200 mL/min alveolar ventilation. B: (250 − 150) × 24 = 2,400 mL/min alveolar ventilation. B has less alveolar ventilation despite the same total ventilation. At unchanged carbon dioxide production, steady-state carbon dioxide tension would tend to rise.
autonomic-signalling: Start with the wiring Both sympathetic and parasympathetic preganglionic neurons release acetylcholine onto neuronal nicotinic receptors. Most sympathetic postganglionic neurons release noradrenaline, whereas most parasympathetic postganglionic neurons release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors. Sympathetic innervation of eccrine sweat glands is an important cholinergic exception. Follow the receptor pathway Many beta-adrenoceptor responses use Gs, adenylyl cyclase and cyclic AMP. Alpha-1 responses commonly use Gq, phospholipase C, IP3 and intracellular calcium. M2 receptors in the heart couple to Gi/o; reduced cyclic AMP and G-protein beta–gamma regulation of potassium channels help slow nodal activity. These are useful dominant pathways, not an exhaustive catalogue. Predict the tissue response The same second messenger can produce different effects in different tissues because the target proteins differ. Beta-1 stimulation supports cardiac rate and force, while beta-2 stimulation can relax bronchial smooth muscle. Name the receptor, cell and effector before predicting a change; avoid treating sympathetic activity as a universal contraction signal. Give a receptor-to-response explanation of slowing at the sinoatrial node. Acetylcholine activates cardiac M2 receptors. Gi/o signalling reduces cyclic AMP, while beta–gamma subunits can activate GIRK potassium channels. These changes reduce pacemaker activity and slow the heart. A learner says every sympathetic postganglionic neuron releases noradrenaline. Which example corrects the claim? Sympathetic fibres to eccrine sweat glands release acetylcholine. Eccrine sweat-gland innervation is the important sympathetic cholinergic exception.
fluid-and-membrane-transport: Separate a gradient from a pathway A concentration gradient can favour movement without providing a route across a membrane. The lipid bilayer limits the movement of most ions and polar solutes. Channels provide selective pores; carriers bind and change conformation. For an ion, both concentration and voltage contribute to its electrochemical gradient. Locate the ATP-consuming step The sodium–potassium ATPase moves three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in per ATP hydrolysed. It maintains the gradients used by excitable cells and transport epithelia. A sodium–glucose cotransporter does not hydrolyse ATP directly: it couples inward sodium movement down its electrochemical gradient to glucose transport. Distinguish osmolarity from tonicity Osmolarity counts dissolved particles per litre of solution. Tonicity predicts the sustained effect on cell volume and depends on solutes that do not readily cross the relevant membrane. A solution can be isosmotic without being isotonic when its solute enters the cell. Always state which membrane and time scale you are considering. Explain how ATP can support glucose uptake without binding to its cotransporter. ATP powers the sodium–potassium pump, which maintains a low intracellular sodium concentration. Sodium then enters through a cotransporter down its electrochemical gradient, providing energy for coupled glucose uptake. The sodium–potassium pump is inhibited in a teaching model. Why might sodium–glucose uptake weaken later? The sodium gradient gradually becomes less able to power cotransport. The pump maintains the gradient; its loss eventually reduces the energy available to secondary transport.
digestive-control: Give the gut a local control loop The enteric nervous system contains interconnected networks in the myenteric and submucosal plexuses. Myenteric circuits are strongly involved in motility, while submucosal circuits help regulate secretion and local blood flow. Autonomic input modifies these circuits. Local sensory input can therefore coordinate a response without requiring every step to be commanded by the brain. Match the hormone to the incoming material Acid arriving in the duodenum stimulates secretin release, supporting pancreatic ductal bicarbonate secretion. Fat and protein digestion products stimulate cholecystokinin, supporting pancreatic enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction. These signals help match the composition of secretions to what the meal requires. Separate mixing, propulsion and absorption Segmentation mainly mixes intestinal contents and increases contact with the mucosa, whereas coordinated peristalsis produces forward propulsion. Digestion breaks macromolecules into absorbable components; absorption moves those components across the epithelium. Pancreatic enzymes, bile-mediated lipid handling and membrane transport each contribute different steps. Explain how a meal containing fat and acid can recruit different pancreatic responses. Duodenal acid stimulates secretin and bicarbonate-rich ductal secretion. Fat and protein products stimulate cholecystokinin and enzyme-rich secretion, with neural signals coordinating the response. The pathways interact rather than operating as isolated switches. Fat enters the duodenum. Which coordinated response fits its digestion? CCK supporting enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction. CCK helps match enzyme and bile delivery to the incoming nutrient load.
ecg-time-and-vectors: Keep the electrical and mechanical stories separate The ECG records changing voltage differences at the body surface. The P wave reflects atrial depolarisation, the QRS complex ventricular depolarisation and the T wave ventricular repolarisation. Atrial repolarisation is usually obscured by the much larger QRS. These are electrical events that precede or overlap mechanical events. A QRS complex is not itself a measurement of ejection or stroke volume, and an electrical tracing alone does not establish effective blood flow. Read the calibration first At a paper speed of 25 mm/s, one 1-mm small square represents 0.04 s and one 5-mm large square represents 0.20 s. At 50 mm/s the same distances represent half those times. Standard voltage calibration is often 10 mm/mV, but it must be checked rather than assumed. For a regular rhythm, heart rate in beats/min = 60 / R–R interval in seconds. Counting large squares with the 300 rule only applies at 25 mm/s. Define the interval endpoints The PR interval starts at P-wave onset and ends at QRS onset. It includes atrial depolarisation and conduction toward the ventricles; it is not simply the duration of the AV node alone. The PR segment begins after the P wave ends. QRS duration measures ventricular depolarisation. The QT interval extends from QRS onset to T-wave end and includes ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation. QT varies with rate, so a raw interval is not interpreted independently of heart rate. Project the vector onto a lead A lead has a positive and a negative direction. A net depolarisation vector toward its positive electrode produces an upward deflection; a vector pointing away produces a downward deflection. A nearly perpendicular vector can produce a small or biphasic signal. The same activation can therefore look different in different leads. Limb leads sample the frontal plane and chest leads the horizontal plane. Begin with calibration, rate, regularity, P-to-QRS relationship and intervals before making an interpretation. Relate P, QRS and T to electrical events. Convert ECG grid distances into time and rate. Predict how a lead records a depolarisation vector. Read a calibrated strip A fictional regular tracing at 25 mm/s has four large squares between successive R peaks and four small squares from P onset to QRS onset. Calculate rate and PR interval. R–R = 4 × 0.20 = 0.80 s. Rate = 60 / 0.80 = 75 beats/min. PR = 4 × 0.04 = 0.16 s. If the speed were 50 mm/s, the same distances would instead represent 150 beats/min and 0.08 s. Calibration is essential.
endocrine-feedback: Name the three levels In the hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid axis, hypothalamic TRH supports pituitary TSH release, and TSH stimulates the thyroid. Thyroid hormones then act on many target tissues. Drawing the levels separately helps distinguish a gland's response to stimulation from the actions of its hormone elsewhere in the body. Close the feedback loop Thyroid hormone feeds back on the hypothalamus and pituitary, reducing stimulation when hormone availability rises. Feedback is a regulatory relationship, not simply a label attached to every endocrine pathway. Some hormones use different controlling variables, and secretion can be pulsatile or follow daily rhythms. Explain a simplified pattern In a simplified primary thyroid-gland failure model, reduced thyroid hormone removes inhibitory feedback and TSH rises if the pituitary can respond. If the defect instead lies centrally, TSH may be low or inappropriately normal despite low thyroid hormone. Real interpretation requires clinical context, assay limitations and other influences; this example teaches the feedback logic. Explain why a target-gland hormone and its pituitary signal can move in opposite directions. A target-gland hormone can inhibit its upstream control signals. When target-gland secretion falls, reduced negative feedback permits the pituitary signal to rise, provided the central components of the axis remain functional. Low thyroid hormone is accompanied by a TSH that is not appropriately elevated. What does this challenge in a simple model? The assumption that the central feedback response is intact. An intact pituitary response to primary thyroid failure would usually raise TSH; central influences merit consideration.
energy-balance: Use a conservation statement Over a defined interval, the change in stored body energy reflects absorbed energy intake minus energy expenditure. Expenditure includes basal cellular work, physical activity and the thermic effect of food. Body mass also changes with water and gastrointestinal contents, so a short-term weight change is not a direct measurement of a change in fat energy. Connect the fed state to storage After a mixed meal, insulin supports storage and use of absorbed nutrients. Glucose can enter insulin-responsive tissues, glycogen stores can be replenished, and lipid storage is favoured. The exact response depends on tissue transporters and metabolic pathways; not every tissue requires insulin for glucose uptake. Connect fasting to mobilisation As the interval since eating increases, a lower insulin-to-glucagon signal supports hepatic glucose production and mobilisation of stored fuels. Glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis contribute on different time scales, while fatty acids supply many tissues. Hormonal control redistributes available fuels; it does not create energy from nothing. Compare nutrient handling after a meal and during fasting. The fed state favours use and storage of absorbed nutrients under a higher insulin signal. Fasting promotes mobilisation of stored fuels and hepatic glucose production under a lower insulin-to-glucagon signal. Energy is transferred and transformed, not created. Which statement best connects fasting to ongoing cellular work? Stored substrates are mobilised to support continued metabolism. Fasting changes fuel sources while tissues continue to use energy.
renal-kidney-map: Two paths, one organ Blood enters a glomerulus through an afferent arteriole and leaves through an efferent arteriole. A second capillary bed receives that blood: peritubular capillaries around cortical tubules, or vasa recta associated with juxtamedullary nephrons. Filtrate crosses into Bowman space and takes a different route through the tubules. Four verbs that keep the map straight Filtration moves fluid and small solutes from glomerular blood into Bowman space. Reabsorption returns material from tubular fluid to blood. Secretion moves material from blood into tubular fluid. Excretion is what finally leaves in urine: filtered amount minus reabsorbed amount plus secreted amount. Location explains function Renal corpuscles lie in the cortex. Long loops of juxtamedullary nephrons extend into the medulla and help establish the concentration gradient. Collecting ducts receive fluid from multiple nephrons and use that gradient when their water permeability increases. Trace the two capillary beds in series. Separate filtration, reabsorption, secretion and excretion. Locate the cortex, medulla and collecting system.
blood-and-haemostasis: Anchor platelets at an injured surface Vascular injury exposes adhesive structures and immobilised von Willebrand factor. Platelet GPIb-IX-V binds von Willebrand factor, while collagen receptors help stabilise adhesion. Platelets then change shape, release mediators and recruit further platelets. Adhesion attaches a platelet to the injured surface; it is not the same event as platelet-to-platelet aggregation. Connect platelets to one another Activation changes the affinity of integrin alpha-IIb-beta-3, also called GPIIb/IIIa. Fibrinogen can bridge these receptors on neighbouring platelets. ADP, thromboxane and thrombin help amplify activation. Platelets also expose a phospholipid surface that supports coagulation-complex assembly, linking primary and secondary haemostasis. Amplify thrombin and stabilise fibrin Intrinsic tenase contains factor IXa with its cofactor VIIIa on a calcium-dependent phospholipid surface; it activates factor X. Factor Xa with Va forms prothrombinase, producing thrombin from prothrombin. Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin, and factor XIIIa crosslinks fibrin. These overlapping processes stabilise the plug; they are not two completely separate timelines. Explain the difference between adhesion, aggregation and fibrin stabilisation. Adhesion anchors platelets to an injured surface. Aggregation joins activated platelets through fibrinogen bridges between alpha-IIb-beta-3 receptors. Coagulation generates thrombin and fibrin, and factor XIIIa crosslinks fibrin to stabilise the plug. A student confuses prothrombinase with intrinsic tenase. Which reaction belongs to prothrombinase? Prothrombin to thrombin. Xa with Va forms prothrombinase and supports thrombin generation.
renal-concentrating-urine: Build the gradient Countercurrent multiplication in the loops of Henle helps establish the corticomedullary osmotic gradient. The descending thin limb permits substantial water movement; the ascending limb recovers salt while restricting water movement. Urea recycling contributes to inner medullary osmolality. Preserve the gradient Vasa recta exchange limits the removal of medullary solute while supplying tissue. Excessive washout weakens the gradient. Countercurrent exchange preserves a gradient; it is not the same mechanism as multiplication in the loop. Open the water route ADH acts on basolateral V2 receptors of collecting-duct principal cells. Gs, cAMP and PKA signaling increases apical AQP2 insertion. Water then moves down an osmotic gradient. With little ADH, low collecting-duct water permeability permits more dilute urine; with ADH and an intact gradient, more water is recovered. Distinguish countercurrent multiplication and exchange. Locate the V2 receptor and AQP2. Explain why ADH needs an intact medullary gradient.
renal-abg-interpretation: Start with pH, but do not stop there For these teaching cases, the arterial pH reference interval is 7.35–7.45, PaCO₂ 35–45 mmHg and bicarbonate 22–26 mmol/L. Acidemia and alkalemia describe the measured pH. Acidosis and alkalosis describe processes: mixed processes may coexist even when pH is inside the reference interval. Read the ratio pH = 6.1 + log₁₀[HCO₃⁻ / (0.03 × PaCO₂)]. A primary fall in bicarbonate drives metabolic acidosis; a primary rise in CO₂ drives respiratory acidosis. The opposite changes drive alkalosis. Compensation moves pH toward the baseline; it should not be assumed simply because both measurements are abnormal. Test the explanation For metabolic acidosis, Winter’s formula gives an expected PaCO₂ of 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8, with a ±2 mmHg range. A measured value above the range suggests an additional respiratory acidosis; below suggests an additional respiratory alkalosis. Also calculate Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻); interpret this anion gap against the laboratory range and albumin. Neither a gap nor an ABG alone establishes a cause. Distinguish acidemia from an acidosis process. Identify the primary change in simple examples. Use expected compensation to recognize a possible additional process.
indicator-dilution: Begin with conservation of the indicator A known amount of indicator is placed into an unknown fluid volume. After mixing, concentration equals the amount remaining divided by that volume. Rearranging gives volume = amount remaining / equilibrated concentration. The indicator should mix throughout the compartment of interest, remain measurable and avoid appreciable entry into other compartments during the measurement. The calculation measures the distribution space of the tracer; naming that space requires understanding its behaviour. Match the tracer to the compartment Labelled water can distribute across cell membranes and therefore estimates total body water. An extracellular marker that is largely excluded from cells estimates extracellular fluid. An indicator retained with plasma proteins estimates plasma volume. Intracellular fluid is usually derived as total body water minus extracellular fluid. Interstitial fluid is approximately extracellular fluid minus plasma volume; whether small transcellular spaces are included depends on the tracer and measurement convention. Correct the numerator before dividing If an indicator is excreted or otherwise lost before the equilibrium sample, subtract that loss from the administered amount. Dividing the full administered amount by a concentration already reduced by loss overestimates volume. Concentration must use units compatible with the dose: milligrams divided by milligrams per litre gives litres. A concentration in milligrams per millilitre instead gives millilitres. Do the unit cancellation explicitly before deciding whether an answer is plausible. Interpret the estimate rather than memorising a person The familiar total-body-water fraction is an illustrative average, not a constant for every person. Body composition and age alter the fractions. A result may also be distorted by sampling before complete mixing, indicator leakage or uncorrected disappearance. Subtraction combines the uncertainty of two measurements. Blood volume and plasma volume are different: in a simplified model, blood volume = plasma volume / (1 − haematocrit), with haematocrit expressed as a fraction. Choose a tracer from the barrier it can cross. Calculate compartment volume after correcting indicator loss. Distinguish measured volume from a volume found by subtraction. A loss-corrected measurement A fictional extracellular tracer dose is 150 mg. By sampling, 10 mg has been lost and the equilibrated concentration is 10 mg/L. Total body water was measured separately as 42 L. Find extracellular and intracellular volumes. Remaining tracer = 150 − 10 = 140 mg. Extracellular volume = 140 mg / 10 mg/L = 14 L. Intracellular volume = 42 − 14 = 28 L. Using 150 mg would give 15 L and overestimate extracellular volume by 1 L.
lymph-and-fluid-exchange: Separate pressure from permeability Capillary hydrostatic pressure favours outward fluid movement. Plasma proteins contribute an opposing colloid osmotic effect, but the endothelial barrier and its glycocalyx determine how those forces act. A pressure change alone does not fully describe exchange when permeability or protein distribution also changes. Include the lymphatic route Lymphatic vessels return filtered interstitial fluid and proteins to the circulation. Sustained venous-end reabsorption is not a universal feature of all systemic capillaries. In many tissues, lymphatic return handles much of the net filtration. Different organs have specialised exchange arrangements, so one diagram should not be treated as a universal map. Build an oedema mechanism Oedema can result when filtration exceeds the capacity for return. Increased venous pressure, increased permeability, reduced plasma protein concentration or impaired lymphatic drainage can contribute through different mechanisms. In a teaching explanation, specify which part changed and then trace its effect; appearance alone does not establish a cause. Explain how venous pressure and lymphatic obstruction can both produce fluid accumulation. Higher venous pressure can increase capillary hydrostatic pressure and filtration. Lymphatic obstruction reduces the route that returns filtered fluid and proteins. Both can increase interstitial fluid, but through different parts of the balance. Two examples cause oedema: increased venous pressure and lymphatic obstruction. What differs? One can increase filtration; the other reduces return. They change different sides of the filtration–return balance.
synaptic-integration: Release a chemical signal An action potential reaching a presynaptic terminal opens voltage-gated calcium channels. Local calcium entry activates the vesicle-fusion machinery, allowing neurotransmitter release into the synaptic cleft. The transmitter then acts on postsynaptic receptors. Calcium links the arriving electrical event to release; it is not the transmitter crossing the cleft. Interpret the postsynaptic conductance change Ionotropic receptors directly regulate channel opening, whereas metabotropic receptors recruit intracellular signalling. Whether an input is excitatory or inhibitory depends on the conductance change, its reversal potential and the receiving cell's state. Inhibitory input can reduce excitability by shunting current even when the membrane does not become much more negative. Combine inputs in time and space Temporal summation combines inputs arriving close together in time. Spatial summation combines inputs from different locations. Dendritic filtering, synapse position and inhibitory conductance shape the result. An action potential is generated when the combined effect reaches the relevant threshold; a single postsynaptic potential need not cause a spike. An action potential and changing conductance Aligned graphs show a neuronal action potential, an early increase in relative sodium conductance and a later, longer potassium conductance increase. Read the two panels together: rapid sodium-channel activation accompanies the upstroke; sodium inactivation and delayed potassium-channel activation support repolarisation. Voltages, timing and conductances are illustrative and vary between cells. This neuronal waveform is not a universal muscle or pacemaker waveform. Distinguish chemical transmission from temporal and spatial summation. Chemical transmission releases a transmitter that changes postsynaptic signalling or conductance. Temporal summation combines closely timed inputs; spatial summation combines inputs at different sites. Their combined effect helps determine whether the receiving neuron fires. Repeated small inputs at the same synapse arrive close together and have a larger combined effect. What is this? Temporal summation. Temporal summation combines effects of closely timed inputs.
renal-renal-acid-base: Reclamation prevents a loss Much filtered bicarbonate is recovered in the proximal tubule. Secreted H⁺ combines with luminal bicarbonate; carbonic anhydrase supports conversion through CO₂ and water. Intracellular reactions permit bicarbonate to return to blood. Recovering filtered bicarbonate prevents its loss, but is not the same as adding new bicarbonate to the body. New bicarbonate needs net acid excretion Acid can leave the body buffered as ammonium or titratable acid, including phosphate-buffered H⁺. Net acid excretion is ammonium excretion plus titratable acid excretion minus urinary bicarbonate loss. Ammoniagenesis is an adaptable component of the renal response to an acid load. A final cellular choice Alpha intercalated cells secrete H⁺ into urine and return bicarbonate to blood. Beta intercalated cells can secrete bicarbonate. These renal adjustments complement lung regulation of CO₂, but full adaptation is slower than the immediate buffering response. Explain filtered bicarbonate reclamation. Connect ammonium and titratable acid excretion to new bicarbonate. Distinguish alpha and beta intercalated cells.
reproductive-cycles: Begin with a coordinated axis Pulsatile hypothalamic GnRH supports pituitary LH and FSH secretion. In the ovary, gonadotrophins support follicular development and steroid production. In the testis, LH supports Leydig-cell testosterone production, while FSH acts on Sertoli cells in support of spermatogenesis. The same pituitary signals act within different tissue arrangements. Connect follicular growth to ovulation Developing ovarian follicles produce estradiol. During most of the cycle, ovarian hormones contribute inhibitory feedback. Sustained sufficiently high estradiol near ovulation can instead generate positive feedback and an LH surge. The surge promotes final oocyte maturation, ovulation and luteinisation. A 28-day diagram is an illustration, not a schedule every person must follow. Match the endometrium to ovarian hormones Estradiol supports proliferative endometrial growth. After ovulation, the corpus luteum produces progesterone, promoting secretory differentiation. If pregnancy does not maintain luteal function, falling progesterone and estradiol contribute to menstruation. Fertilisation usually occurs in the uterine-tube ampulla; implantation is a later, distinct event in the uterus. Relate the ovarian and endometrial phases without assuming a fixed calendar. Follicular estradiol supports endometrial proliferation. A sustained estradiol rise can trigger an LH surge and ovulation. Luteal progesterone supports secretory endometrium; falling luteal hormones contribute to menstruation when pregnancy does not maintain the corpus luteum. After ovulation, which hormone most directly supports secretory differentiation of the endometrium? Progesterone from the corpus luteum. Luteal progesterone supports secretory changes following estradiol-driven proliferation.
membrane-potentials: Create the resting voltage Concentration gradients and selective permeability determine membrane potential. In many resting excitable cells, potassium permeability strongly influences the voltage. The sodium–potassium pump maintains the gradients and also has a smaller direct electrogenic effect. Cross threshold In a simplified neuronal model, depolarization opens voltage-gated sodium channels, producing regenerative inward current. An action potential is all-or-none for a given cell under specified conditions; stronger sustained stimulation is often encoded through frequency rather than endlessly larger spikes. Recover excitability Sodium-channel inactivation and delayed potassium current support repolarization. Recovery from inactivation underlies refractory behavior. Channel contributions differ among neurons, skeletal muscle, working cardiac cells and pacemaker cells; one waveform does not represent all excitable tissues. An action potential and changing conductance Aligned graphs show a neuronal action potential, an early increase in relative sodium conductance and a later, longer potassium conductance increase. Read the two panels together: rapid sodium-channel activation accompanies the upstroke; sodium inactivation and delayed potassium-channel activation support repolarisation. Voltages, timing and conductances are illustrative and vary between cells. This neuronal waveform is not a universal muscle or pacemaker waveform.
special-senses: Light reduces photoreceptor depolarisation In darkness, cyclic-GMP-dependent channels support the photoreceptor dark current. Light activates the phototransduction cascade, reducing cyclic GMP and closing these channels. The photoreceptor hyperpolarises and releases less glutamate. This is a graded receptor response; it is not a conventional all-or-none action potential in the rod or cone. Hair bundles gate a mechanically sensitive current Deflection of a sensory hair bundle in its excitatory direction opens mechanotransduction channels. Potassium-rich endolymph and the electrochemical arrangement favour an inward current that depolarises the hair cell. This changes calcium entry and transmitter release to sensory afferents. Deflection in the opposite direction reduces the response. Keep the sensory code and route separate Cochlear position helps encode sound frequency because different parts of the basilar membrane respond best to different frequencies. Vestibular organs instead contribute information about head movement and orientation. A complete explanation names the stimulus, receptor response, transmitter change and afferent pathway, rather than saying that every sensory receptor fires in the same way. Compare the direction of the initial receptor response to light and to excitatory hair-bundle deflection. Light closes cyclic-GMP-gated channels and hyperpolarises a photoreceptor. Excitatory hair-bundle deflection opens mechanically gated channels and depolarises a hair cell. Both graded responses regulate transmitter release. A hair bundle is deflected in its excitatory direction. Which initial response is expected? Opening of mechanotransduction channels and depolarisation. Mechanical channel opening permits a depolarising current under the inner-ear ionic conditions.
cardiac-output: Define each quantity Stroke volume is end-diastolic volume minus end-systolic volume. Cardiac output equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume. Ejection fraction divides stroke volume by end-diastolic volume. The quantities describe different aspects of pumping and have different units. Change filling Increased venous return can increase end-diastolic filling and preload. Within physiological limits, length-dependent activation increases force and stroke volume: the Frank–Starling mechanism. This is not the same as an increase in intrinsic contractility. Change the pump state Contractility describes changes in force generation at a given starting length and loading context. Sympathetic beta1 signaling can increase inotropy. Afterload also affects ejection, so a change in ejection fraction cannot automatically be assigned to one mechanism. Compare ventricular pressure–volume loops Four qualitative left-ventricular pressure–volume panels compare the normal cycle and isolated changes in preload, afterload and contractility. Grey loops are the control. Compare width (stroke volume) and end-systolic position when one variable changes. These are isolated qualitative changes; physiological systems often change several variables together. The loops are not patient measurements.
baroreflex: Sense stretch Carotid-sinus and aortic-arch receptors respond to stretch associated with arterial pressure. Carotid signals travel predominantly through the glossopharyngeal pathway; aortic signals travel through the vagus. These are sensory inputs, not the final autonomic outputs. Integrate the change The medullary network, including nucleus tractus solitarius, adjusts autonomic activity. A rise in arterial pressure generally increases baroreceptor signaling, increases cardiac vagal influence and reduces sympathetic outflow. A fall produces the opposite compensatory tendency. Act on heart and vessels Changes in heart rate, contractility and vascular tone buffer the pressure disturbance. This is rapid feedback, not a complete account of long-term pressure control. Distinguish the arterial reflex from atrial stretch responses associated with increased venous return.
cardiac-cycle: Use pressure differences to order the cycle During filling, atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure and the atrioventricular valve is open. As ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure, that valve closes. Before ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure, both valves are closed: pressure rises at almost constant volume. The arterial valve opens when the ventricular-to-arterial pressure difference favours ejection. Read the loop rather than its shape alone The width of a ventricular pressure–volume loop is stroke volume: end-diastolic minus end-systolic volume. Its area represents external stroke work. Isovolumetric contraction and relaxation are nearly vertical because volume changes little while pressure changes. Real measurements depend on loading conditions and valve function; a teaching loop simplifies these details. Change one variable at a time With other conditions held fixed, increased filling can raise stroke volume through the Frank–Starling mechanism. An isolated increase in afterload tends to increase end-systolic volume and reduce stroke volume on that beat. Increased contractility tends to reduce end-systolic volume. In an intact circulation, reflexes and subsequent filling can change the later response. Compare ventricular pressure–volume loops Four qualitative left-ventricular pressure–volume panels compare the normal cycle and isolated changes in preload, afterload and contractility. Grey loops are the control. Compare width (stroke volume) and end-systolic position when one variable changes. These are isolated qualitative changes; physiological systems often change several variables together. The loops are not patient measurements. Predict the immediate effect of an isolated afterload increase on a pressure–volume loop. At unchanged preload and contractility, the ventricle must develop more pressure before ejection. It generally ejects less on that beat, leaving a larger end-systolic volume and a narrower loop. Later reflex and filling responses may modify this. In a simplified ventricle, end-diastolic volume is 120 mL and end-systolic volume is 50 mL. What is stroke volume? 70 mL. Subtract end-systolic from end-diastolic volume: 120 minus 50 equals 70 mL.
muscle-contraction: Skeletal muscle: activate the thin filament At the neuromuscular junction, acetylcholine produces an end-plate depolarisation that can initiate a muscle action potential. In skeletal muscle, the T-tubule voltage sensor couples to sarcoplasmic-reticulum calcium release. Calcium binds troponin C, moving the tropomyosin constraint on actin–myosin interaction. ATP supports cross-bridge cycling and calcium reuptake. Cardiac muscle: trigger calcium-induced release In cardiac working myocytes, calcium entering through L-type channels triggers further calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Troponin C again regulates the thin filament. The prolonged action potential and refractory period strongly limit summation into tetanus, allowing filling between contractions. This working-myocyte model differs from nodal pacemaker activity. Smooth muscle: regulate myosin Smooth muscle uses calcium–calmodulin to activate myosin light-chain kinase. Phosphorylation of myosin supports interaction with actin; myosin light-chain phosphatase favours relaxation. Smooth muscle lacks the troponin switch used in striated muscle. Stretch, local signals and autonomic input can regulate force, sometimes without a full action potential. Compare the role of calcium in skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle. Skeletal and cardiac muscle use troponin C to regulate actin access. Skeletal coupling primarily releases stored calcium through voltage-sensor coupling; cardiac muscle needs trigger calcium entry. Smooth muscle uses calcium–calmodulin and myosin light-chain kinase to regulate myosin. Why can normal skeletal muscle produce tetanic force while normal cardiac working muscle cannot? The cardiac refractory period overlaps much of its contraction. The long refractory period limits repeated excitation and summation into tetanus, preserving filling between beats.
ventilation-perfusion: Deliver air and blood Ventilation brings fresh gas to alveoli; perfusion brings blood to pulmonary capillaries. Effective exchange depends on their regional matching. Minute ventilation includes dead-space ventilation, so it does not directly equal fresh gas reaching exchange surfaces. Compare the limiting patterns Very low ventilation relative to perfusion approaches a shunt-like pattern. Ventilation without perfusion is dead space. These are different ways to waste one side of the exchange system; neither is explained solely by membrane thickness. Add diffusion and transport Gas crosses the barrier down partial-pressure gradients. Surface area, diffusion distance and gas properties affect transfer. Oxygen content then depends strongly on hemoglobin as well as saturation and dissolved oxygen; a partial pressure is not itself a complete oxygen-content measurement. Conducting airways and gas-exchanging alveoli Conducting airways are coloured red, alveoli blue; an inset shows surrounding capillaries and a conceptual oxygen and nitrogen washout graph. The conducting zone carries gas; gas exchange begins in the respiratory zone. In the source’s washout key, horizontal position means exhaled volume and vertical position means relative gas concentration. The solid red oxygen-rich signal falls while the dashed blue nitrogen signal rises after breathing oxygen. The graph is qualitative, without calibrated axes; do not use it to calculate dead-space volume.
respiratory-mechanics: Create a pressure gradient During quiet inspiration, diaphragm contraction expands the thorax. Alveolar pressure transiently falls below atmospheric pressure, so air flows inward. Airflow stops when the pressures equalise. Quiet expiration is mainly driven by elastic recoil. The diaphragm receives motor supply through the phrenic nerves, principally from C3–C5. Distinguish pressure from resistance For a simplified airway, airflow equals the pressure difference divided by airway resistance. At the same pressure difference, doubling resistance halves airflow. Use this relationship to interpret the pressure diagram and resistance question below. Subtract the non-exchanging volume Minute ventilation equals tidal volume multiplied by respiratory rate. Alveolar ventilation is approximated by (tidal volume minus dead-space volume) multiplied by rate, using consistent units. Anatomic dead space is conducting-airway volume; alveolar dead space is ventilation that receives little or no effective perfusion. Compare two fictional breathing patterns With a fixed dead space of 150 mL, 500 mL breaths at 12/min give 4.2 L/min alveolar ventilation. Breaths of 300 mL at 20/min give only 3.0 L/min, despite the same 6.0 L/min minute ventilation. This is a simplified teaching calculation. Actual dead space and carbon-dioxide production vary; these examples are not ventilation prescriptions. Conducting airways and gas-exchanging alveoli Conducting airways are coloured red, alveoli blue; an inset shows surrounding capillaries and a conceptual oxygen and nitrogen washout graph. The conducting zone carries gas; gas exchange begins in the respiratory zone. In the source’s washout key, horizontal position means exhaled volume and vertical position means relative gas concentration. The solid red oxygen-rich signal falls while the dashed blue nitrogen signal rises after breathing oxygen. The graph is qualitative, without calibrated axes; do not use it to calculate dead-space volume. Explain why rapid shallow breaths can be less efficient than slower deeper breaths at the same minute ventilation. A fixed conducting-airway volume takes up more of each small breath. After subtracting dead space, less fresh air reaches gas-exchanging alveoli each minute, even when total minute ventilation is unchanged. At the same 6 L/min minute ventilation and a fixed 150 mL dead space, which pattern gives greater alveolar ventilation? 500 mL at 12 breaths/min. This gives (500−150)×12 = 4.2 L/min, because less of total ventilation is wasted in dead space.
renal-volume-and-osmolality: How much versus how concentrated Extracellular volume is closely linked to total body sodium content. Osmolality describes the number of dissolved particles relative to water. Plasma sodium concentration therefore reflects the relationship between solute and water, rather than directly measuring total sodium stores or circulating volume. Respond to low effective circulation Reduced renal perfusion, low NaCl delivery at the macula densa and renal sympathetic β1 stimulation can promote renin release. Angiotensin II supports vascular tone, sodium recovery, thirst and aldosterone secretion. Effective circulating volume describes how adequately the arterial circulation is filled, not merely the amount of fluid visible in tissues. Choose the hormone by the job Aldosterone increases distal sodium recovery and supports potassium secretion. ADH chiefly regulates collecting-duct water permeability. Increased osmolality stimulates thirst and ADH; a substantial fall in effective circulating volume can also stimulate ADH, even when osmotic signals would otherwise suppress it. Distinguish extracellular volume from concentration. Identify signals for renin release. Contrast aldosterone and ADH actions.
renal-water-balance: Identify the regulated variable Osmolality describes the concentration of osmotically active particles, whereas extracellular volume reflects the amount of fluid in that compartment. Sodium balance is a major determinant of extracellular volume; water balance strongly influences osmolality. The two variables interact, but an explanation should identify which change is driving the response. Use ADH to alter water permeability ADH binds basolateral V2 receptors on collecting-duct principal cells and promotes insertion of aquaporin-2 into the apical membrane. Water can then move into the hyperosmotic medullary interstitium. ADH uses the gradient; it does not create the entire countercurrent system by itself. Both osmotic signals and sufficiently strong volume signals can regulate its release. Use aldosterone to adjust sodium and potassium handling Aldosterone promotes sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion in responsive distal nephron cells by altering transport proteins, including epithelial sodium channels and the sodium–potassium ATPase. Angiotensin II and plasma potassium are important regulators. Predicting water retention additionally requires attention to water permeability, intake and the other control systems. Distinguish what ADH changes from what aldosterone changes. ADH increases collecting-duct water permeability through aquaporin-2 trafficking. Aldosterone enhances distal sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. Their effects interact with medullary gradients, intake and circulating-volume signals. ADH rises, but the medullary osmotic gradient is greatly reduced. What limits water recovery? Increased permeability still needs an osmotic driving force. ADH makes a pathway available; the medullary gradient supplies the driving force.
renal-filtration-and-clearance: A virtual volume, not a drained container Clearance is the volume of plasma that would contain the amount of a substance excreted each minute. C = U × V / P. If urine concentration is 100 mg/mL, urine flow is 1 mL/min and plasma concentration is 1 mg/mL, clearance is 100 mL/min. The concentrations must use matching units. Choose the marker by its handling Inulin is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so its clearance equals GFR under ideal measurement conditions. Creatinine is convenient but is also secreted slightly, so measured creatinine clearance tends to overestimate GFR. At low concentrations, PAH is filtered and strongly secreted; its clearance approximates effective renal plasma flow, because extraction is high but incomplete. Ask what the denominator contains Filtration fraction is GFR divided by renal plasma flow. For GFR 120 mL/min and RPF 600 mL/min, FF is 0.20, or 20%. Blood flow includes cells: RBF = RPF / (1 − hematocrit). Using PAH clearance in place of true RPF gives an estimate based on effective plasma flow. Calculate clearance from urine concentration, flow and plasma concentration. Explain why inulin, creatinine and PAH give different information. Calculate filtration fraction without confusing blood and plasma flow.
